claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its subsets are governed by stacking fault energy.
Stacking fault energy influences whether dislocation slip or deformation twinning is the dominant deformation mechanism.
Lower stacking fault energy promotes greater twinning activity.
Increased twinning activity enhances strain hardening.
Higher stacking fault energy favors dislocation-slip-dominated deformation.
Dislocation-slip dominance leads to higher yield strength.
Dislocation-slip dominance leads to lower ductility.
Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni subsets having higher Mn or Co content will have lower stacking fault energy than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Subsets with lower stacking fault energy will have higher strain hardening than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Subsets with lower stacking fault energy will have higher ductility than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni subsets having higher Ni or Fe content will have higher stacking fault energy than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Subsets with higher stacking fault energy will have higher yield strength than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Subsets with higher stacking fault energy will have lower ductility than the equiatomic quinary alloy.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys in the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system under room-temperature deformation.
At elevated temperatures, mechanisms such as creep may dominate and invalidate the proposed relationship.
The quantitative relationship between stacking fault energy and mechanical properties in these alloys is not well established.
Short-range ordering or local chemical heterogeneity may also influence the mechanical properties.
